Although mortality rates from pneumonia have declined over the past two decades, neonatal pneumonia continues to be a global health issue that disproportionately affects developing countries.115 At autopsy, pneumonia, diagnosed by the presence of inflammation, has been diagnosed in 20% to 60% of stillbirths and liveborn neonatal deaths.116
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: Neonatal pneumonia is classified as early, presenting within the first week of life, or late, presenting after 7 days of life. Congenital pneumonia is one subset of early pneumonia that is acquired in utero and usually presents immediately after delivery. Congenital pneumonia is acquired through aspiration of infected amniotic fluid, ascending infection through intact or ruptured membranes, or hematogenous spread through the placenta. Early pneumonia can also be acquired during labor secondary to aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or bacteria colonizing the birth canal. Late neonatal pneumonia, which includes ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), is usually a nosocomial infection and occurs most commonly in ventilated neonates, although infection through hematogenous spread can also occur.
paragraphs.heading: Etiology

paragraphs.text: Whereas bacterial, viral, and fungal agents can cause pneumonia, the etiologic agent is usually related to the timing of occurrence of pneumonia. The pathogens responsible for early onset pneumonia mirror those of early-onset sepsis. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the most common cause of early pneumonia in term babies. However, the overall incidence of GBS sepsis has decreased dramatically since the introduction of universal screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.117 Most recently, the incidence of gram-negative sepsis, especially that caused by Escherichia coli, which is ampicillin resistant, has increased overall and now is the most common pathogen in the very low birth weight (VLBW) population.118 Other bacterial causes of pneumonia include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, group A streptococci, Staphylococcus, and Listeria monocytogenes. Anaerobes such as Bacteroides are occasionally recovered, but the contribution of these organisms to early-onset pneumonia is minimal.
paragraphs.heading: Etiology

paragraphs.text: Herpes simplex is the major cause of early viral pneumonia and is usually acquired during labor. Pneumonia is associated with disseminated herpes infection and is usually associated with a high mortality rate. Other causes of early viral pneumonia include adenovirus, enterovirus, mumps, and rubella, whereas early pneumonia is an unusual presentation of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. Other TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, other [such as syphilis], rubella, CMV, and herpes simplex virus) can also present with early-onset pneumonia. Up to 70% of disseminated candidal infections are associated with pneumonia, especially in premature infants.
paragraphs.heading: Etiology

paragraphs.text: Late-onset pneumonia is usually caused by organisms that colonize the newborn during the hospital stay. These include Staphylococcus species, including coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, E. coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, Enterobacter cloacae, Pseudomonas, Bacillus cereus, and Citrobacter, all of which can cause severe pneumonia, especially in preterm infants. When Chlamydia trachomatis infection is acquired during labor, it usually manifests as pneumonia at 2 to 4 weeks of life because of its long incubation period. Viral causes of late-onset pneumonia include respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, human mentapneumovirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza, and influenza A and B, as well as coronavirus.119 CMV pneumonia should always be considered in babies with congenital infection presenting with late respiratory decompensation. Prolonged courses of antibiotics and corticosteroids can increase the risk of candidal pneumonia, especially in colonized infants with extremely low birth weight (ELBW).
paragraphs.heading: Etiology

paragraphs.text: Risk factors for early pneumonia are similar to those for neonatal sepsis and include prematurity, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS colonization, chorioamnionitis, and intrapartum maternal fever. However, in one study, 22% of neonatal cases did not have risk factors, and, in almost half, the only risk factor was early onset of labor. Therefore risk factors should not determine whether to start antibiotics in neonates with respiratory distress, especially infants with ELBW. The duration of mechanical ventilation, low birth weight, and prematurity are the main risk factors for development of late-onset pneumonia.119 Other risk factors include abnormal neurologic conditions predisposing to aspiration pneumonia, poor nutrition, severe underlying disease, and prolonged hospitalization.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Clinical manifestations of early-onset pneumonia can be nonspecific; therefore a high index of suspicion should always be exercised. These symptoms include temperature instability, lethargy, apnea, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, abdominal distention, poor feeding, and neurologic depression. Respiratory distress can present in the form of tachypnea and retractions in more than two-thirds of affected neonates. Cough is an unusual symptom in neonatal pneumonia and was present in fewer than one-third of
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: neonates.120 Delay in diagnosis and treatment can lead to PPHN and septic shock.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Differential diagnosis for early neonatal pneumonia includes transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), RDS, MAS, and pulmonary congestion secondary to obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous return or other left heart obstructive lesions. Radiographic findings characteristic of pneumonia are nonspecific and thus do not help differentiate pneumonia from the disorders mentioned in the preceding. Chest x-ray findings might include unilateral or bilateral streaky densities, confluent mottled opacified areas, or a diffusely granular appearance with air bronchograms. Differentiation from RDS is difficult in preterm infants, especially because preterm labor is a risk factor for pneumonia. Radiographic findings of TTN usually resolve by 48 hours, and those of RDS are markedly improved after surfactant treatment, whereas radiologic changes of pneumonia may persist for weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Late-onset pneumonia usually presents with nonspecific changes in the overall condition of the infant in the form of new-onset or increased apnea, abdominal distension or feeding intolerance, temperature instability, respiratory distress, hyperglycemia, or cardiovascular instability. Patients receiving ventilatory assistance usually present with an increased oxygen requirement or mechanical support.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of pneumonia requires a high index of suspicion in any infant with new onset of symptoms suggestive of sepsis. Sepsis work-up, including blood culture, blood count, and differential, should be obtained before starting antibiotics. Laboratory findings such as leukopenia or leukocytosis can be a helpful. Tracheal Gram stain and culture should be considered in infants who require mechanical ventilation. Results demonstrating leukocytes and a predominant organism can aide in antimicrobial therapy. Analysis and culture of pleural fluid, if present in an adequate amount, can aid in the diagnosis in infants not responding to empiric therapy. Specific studies for viral or unusual bacterial infections should be obtained if suspected. Diagnosis of VAP can be troublesome, especially in preterm infants with underlying lung disease. Typically, these infants’ tracheas are colonized, discounting the validity of tracheal cultures. More recently, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Health Safety Network (NHSN) proposed a surveillance algorithm to define ventilator-associated events (VAEs) that relies on a sustained increased in ventilator and oxygen support after a period of baseline stability to track adverse ventilator events. However, these are not meant to be used to define and treat pneumonia.121 Further studies are clearly needed to better diagnose and treat pneumonia in ventilated infants with low birth weight.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Successful treatment depends on identification of the causative organism, institution of early and adequate antibiotic therapy, and supportive care. Empirical antibiotic therapy is usually started before isolation of the organism. In
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: early-onset pneumonia, ampicillin and gentamicin are adequate initial therapy. However, with the increasing incidence of antibiotic-resistant gram-negative bacteria, this regimen may have to be altered based on specific institutional susceptibility data. For late-onset pneumonia, initial antibiotic choice may depend on prior infections or colonization of the infant, as well as resistance patterns in the institution. Empiric therapy aimed to cover drug-resistant gram-negative and gram-positive organisms includes vancomycin for methicillin-resistant S. aureus. When the causative organism is isolated, specific therapy is started based on the susceptibility profile. The duration of therapy is dependent on the causative organism and response to treatment; however, in uncomplicated pneumonia, 10 to 14 days of therapy are usually adequate.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Whereas antibiotic therapy is the mainstay of treatment, supportive care is essential and has been shown to decrease the mortality and morbidity associated with pneumonia in developing countries. In the acute stage, circulatory support with fluids and inotropes might be needed, and mechanical ventilation and oxygen should be administered to correct hypoxemia. Special attention to correct acidosis, hypoglycemia, and other possible electrolyte imbalance is also warranted. Nutritional support with either parenteral nutrition or enteral feeds when clinically appropriate should be provided.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: TTN is a common physiologic disorder of the newborn resulting from pulmonary edema secondary to inadequate or delayed clearance of fetal alveolar fluid. The initial clinical picture is usually completely resolved by 48 to 72 hours, thus the term transient. However, TTN continues to represent a diagnostic dilemma secondary to the inability to differentiate its initial presentation from that of other causes of respiratory distress, including pneumonia. The incidence has been estimated at 5.7 per 1000 births in term infants. Risk factors for development of TTN include premature or elective cesarean delivery without labor, small for gestational age, macrosomia, maternal diabetes, maternal asthma, maternal hypertension, twin pregnancy, and male gender.122 The incidence of pulmonary pathology including TTN was found to be two- to threefold higher in infants born after planned cesarean delivery compared with a planned vaginal delivery.123
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: Fetal alveolar fluid is continuously secreted during pregnancy through an epithelial chloride secretion mechanism, and the rate of secretion decreases a few days before delivery. At birth, the balance of fluid movement in the alveolus switches from chloride secretion to sodium absorption, causing resorption of intra-alveolar fluid. Absorption occurs in two steps. First, sodium moves from the alveolar lumen into the cell by passive movement across a concentration gradient maintained by the Na-K-ATPase pump. Next, sodium is actively transported into the interstitium by
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: amiloride-sensitive epithelial sodium channels (ENaCs). Thereafter, the sodium and fluid are cleared through the lymphatic and vascular systems.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: The mechanisms underlying failure or delay in clearance of intra-alveolar fluid in patients with TTN are not totally understood. The mechanical force of birth canal squeeze, originally thought to be the major factor in lung fluid resorption, is now believed to be only a minor contributor. Immaturity of ENaCs has been shown, both in animals and in neonates, to impair fluid resorption and, as ENaC expression is developmentally regulated, this is especially relevant in the late preterm infant. Hormonal changes associated with spontaneous labor, especially the surge of catecholamines and endogenous steroids, and activation of the β-adrenergic system, seem to be important in increasing the expression and activity of ENaC, which partially accounts for the higher incidence of TTN in elective cesarean section cases not preceded by spontaneous labor.124
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: The clinical picture of patients with TTN is secondary to the decrease in lung compliance associated with pulmonary edema. Collapse of airways might also occur in response to fluid accumulation in the interstitium and peribronchial lymphatics. The net result is variable degrees of hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: Patients with TTN usually present very early after birth with symptoms of respiratory distress. Tachypnea is the most consistent finding, although increased work of breathing with expiratory grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions may also be present. Hypoxemia necessitating modest oxygen requirement (usually <40%), together with hypercapnia, can occur, whereas respiratory failure requiring CPAP is unusual. The most characteristic feature of TTN is the transient nature of this disease. In most patients, rapid continuous improvement in the clinical condition occurs within 24 to 48 hours of life, although in some patients, symptoms might persist beyond 72 hours of life. Characteristic radiographic findings consist of perihilar streaking that represents engorgement of the periarterial lymphatics and fluid-filled interlobar fissures. Both the horizontal and oblique fissures can be affected, although the horizontal is affected more commonly. Fluid-filled alveoli can present as fluffy bilateral infiltrates. Atelectasis and pleural effusion can also be seen. Although these radiographic changes can readily be distinguished from classic changes of RDS, TTN can conceivably accompany RDS in preterm infants. Radiographic changes are improved by 48 hours; however, they may not appear normal for 7 days. Ultrasound has recently been described to be useful in the diagnosis of TTN, as well as in prediction of the need for respiratory support in infants affected by TTN. Ultrasound findings consistent with TTN include thickening of the pleural line, disappearance of A-lines, and appearance of B-lines. A sharp demarcation between the echogenicity of the upper and lower lung fields, referred to as the double lung point, can also be seen with TTN but is not essential.125-127
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: Treatment of TTN is supportive. However, because it is difficult to differentiate TTN from other disorders, most patients are usually started on antibiotics that can be discontinued after 36 to 48 hours if cultures are negative and the diagnosis is more clear. Lasix has no role in the treatment of TTN. The use of antenatal steroids prior to late preterm delivery has demonstrated decreased rates of TTN among other respiratory morbidities,128 perhaps through enhanced fluid resorption from alveolar spaces through increased transcription and activation of ENaCs. However, this is not practiced beyond 36 6/7 weeks’ gestation. Exogenous steroids or catecholamines do not seem to provide benefit after birth when the patient becomes symptomatic, because recovery usually precedes the action of these agents. Salbutamol may reduce the duration of tachypnea compared to placebo, but it is unclear if it reduces the need for mechanical ventilator support.129 Delaying elective cesarean section until 39 to 40 weeks’ gestation or until spontaneous labor starts will decrease the incidence of TTN. However, this should be weighed against possible complications of delaying a needed cesarean section.130 Although TTN is considered a self-limited transient condition, there are increasing data to suggest that TTN increases a newborn’s risk for developing a wheezing syndrome early in life.131
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary hemorrhage is an acute, life-threatening complication in neonates, especially ELBW infants, and has been associated with higher morbidity and mortality. It characteristically occurs in infants who are ventilated after they have received surfactant and have a sudden gush of blood or hemorrhagic edema through the endotracheal tube associated with a worsening clinical picture requiring increased ventilatory support and blood product transfusion.132,133 The incidence of such severe hemorrhage is about one to 12 per 1000 live births, and up to 4% to 12% of VLBW infants.134 Risk factors for development of pulmonary hemorrhage include extreme prematurity, surfactant administration, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with left-to-right shunting, multiple birth, early-onset sepsis, and lower 1and 5-minute Apgar scores.133,135 More than 80% of cases of serious pulmonary hemorrhage occur before 72 hours of life with a median of 40 hours; however, some babies might present after 1 week of life.136
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: The pathophysiology of pulmonary hemorrhage is believed to be secondary to a sudden decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance, causing increased left-to-right shunting and pulmonary vascular engorgement, pulmonary edema, and, ultimately, rupture of pulmonary capillaries. This is especially true in patients with a PDA after surfactant treatment. In a post hoc analysis of patients enrolled in the trial for indomethacin prophylaxis in premature infants, a reduced risk for PDA accounted for 80% of the beneficial effect of prophylactic indomethacin on serious pulmonary bleeds.137 However, pulmonary hemorrhage can also occur in patients who never received surfactant or had a PDA,
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: highlighting the importance of other etiologies in the pathogenesis of pulmonary hemorrhage, including aggressive suctioning, especially using a closed-circuit system.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Patients with pulmonary hemorrhage usually present with cyanosis, bradycardia, apnea, gasping, hypotension, increased work of breathing, hypoxia, and hypercapnia, requiring increased ventilatory support. In almost one-third of patients, serious pulmonary hemorrhage was preceded by prodromal episodes of suctioning frothy blood-tinged tracheal secretions. Chest radiographs demonstrate acute and varying degrees of worsening of the underlying pulmonary disease, ranging from bilateral fluffy infiltrates to complete whiteout in severe cases.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Treatment of pulmonary hemorrhage is mostly supportive. Increased ventilatory support, especially increasing mean airway pressure (MAP), serves two purposes: It is needed for adequate ventilation and oxygenation, and it acts to stop the bleeding. A recent systematic review has found that surfactant therapy, HFOV, and increasing MAP are successful evidence-based treatments. Other potentially useful therapies include increased positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), instillation of epinephrine via the endotracheal tube, and treatment of any bleeding and coagulopathy with blood product administration.132 However, more randomized trials comparing different treatments are needed to prove benefit.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary hemorrhage is associated with mortality approaching 50% in ELBW infants. Whereas initial retrospective studies did not show worse neurodevelopmental outcomes in survivors of pulmonary hemorrhage, one study showed increased incidence of cerebral palsy and cognitive delay (odds ratios = 2.86 and 2.4, respectively).137 Pulmonary hemorrhage was also associated with increased incidence of periventricular leukomalacia and seizures at 18 months of age.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Air leak occurs more commonly in the newborn period than any other period of life. One to two percent of all live births of term infants were found to have a pneumothorax on consecutive chest radiographs in 1930. In a recent analysis, the Kids’ Inpatients Database (KID) found an increased incidence of neonatal pneumothorax with decreasing gestational age, highest in ≤24 weeks’ gestational age. The odds of mortality associated with pneumothorax was greatest between 29 and 32 weeks’ gestational age. The diagnosis of pneumothorax was also associated with increased length of hospital stay.138 Air-leak syndromes include pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE), and pneumopericardium, and less commonly, pneumoperitoneum and subcutaneous emphysema. Even though air leaks can occur spontaneously, they mostly occur in patients with lung pathology, including MAS, pneumonia, RDS, diaphragmatic hernia, and pulmonary hypoplasia, especially when positive-pressure ventilation is required. The introduction
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Air Leak Syndromes

paragraphs.text: of surfactant for treatment of RDS has caused a decrease in the incidence of air leaks.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Air Leak Syndromes

paragraphs.text: Air leaks occur when overdistended alveoli rupture into the perivascular bundle, from where air tracks toward the hilum or pleura, causing pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax, respectively. In the preterm infant in whom the interstitium is more abundant and less dissectible, air can stay in the perivascular sheets, causing PIE. Alveolar overdistension might occur in the presence of uneven alveolar ventilation or air trapping. Atelectasis in RDS and plugged small airways in MAS cause unequal distribution of the ventilated volume and transpulmonary pressure to the more distensible areas of the lung, increasing the risk of rupture and air leak. Partial obstruction during MAS causes air trapping when inspired air is not completely evacuated during exhalation. Further accumulation during subsequent breaths can rupture the alveolar space.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Different ventilatory strategies have been associated with the development of pneumothorax, including higher PIP especially in the 24 hours preceding pneumothorax, long inspiratory time (>0.5 seconds), and frequent suctioning in the 8 hours before pneumothorax. Elective initial use of high nasal CPAP (8 cm H2O) in infants at 25 to 28 weeks’ gestation was associated with increased incidence of air leak from 3% to 9% when compared with intubated infants who received surfactant therapy. However, there was no difference in the incidence of BPD or mortality rate between the two groups.139 Use of CPAP (5 cm H2O) in the delivery room in extremely low gestational age infants was associated with a decreased need for intubation and postnatal corticosteroids for BPD and fewer days of mechanical ventilation when compared with initial intubation and surfactant administration within 1 hour after birth, without an increase in the incidence of pneumothorax.140 However, the use of CPAP in the delivery room has been associated with an increased odds of pneumothorax in term and late-preterm infants.141 Factors possibly associated with decreased incidence of pneumothorax include positive-pressure ventilation (rate >60) and volume-targeted ventilation. The use of HFOV following pneumothorax was associated with a decreased incidence of secondary pneumothorax.142
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Although pneumothorax can be the presenting diagnosis, more commonly it complicates underlying lung pathology. Sudden worsening in respiratory distress should always raise the suspicion of the development of a pneumothorax. Tachypnea, grunting, flaring, and retractions occur most commonly. Hypoxemia with cyanosis and increased oxygen requirement occur early in the course of pneumothorax, and hypercapnia follows. Hypoxemia develops secondary to hypoventilation and ventilation-perfusion mismatch as the affected lung collapses. Physical examination reveals distant breath sounds, overdistension of the chest wall, and bulging abdomen on the affected side secondary to downward
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: displacement of the diaphragm in patients with unilateral pneumothorax. The cardiac apex is displaced away from the affected side, as is the trachea.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Larger volumes of leaked air can cause significant increase in intrathoracic pressure, which impairs venous blood return and compromises cardiac output, causing poor tissue perfusion and metabolic acidosis. Although bradycardia and hypotension were not seen in a piglet model of moderate pneumothorax (30 mL of air), they can develop with a severe tension pneumothorax. The decreased cardiac output may cause a compensatory increase in carotid blood flow as the body tries to protect vital organs. The resultant increase in cerebral blood flow together with impairment of cerebral venous return secondary to increased central venous pressure might explain the increased incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) in patients with pneumothorax.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Pneumomediastinum is often asymptomatic if not associated with pneumothorax and is mostly found on radiographic evaluation of patients with respiratory distress or distant heart sounds. Dissection of air through the anterior mediastinum into the neck can cause subcutaneous emphysema that is most commonly felt as subcutaneous crepitus in the face, neck, or supraclavicular notch area.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Pneumopericardium is a rare and serious complication probably caused by dissection of leaked air through the vascular bundle of the great vessels. Trapped air in the limited pericardial space can quickly cause cardiac tamponade, decreasing venous return and cardiac output. Pneumopericardium should be suspected in patients with an air leak and sudden cardiovascular compromise associated with a narrow pulse pressure. The clinical picture consists of worsening respiratory distress, hypotension, bradycardia, pallor, and/or cyanosis. Cardiac sounds are distant or muffled on auscultation, and a pericardial rub might also be heard. Low-voltage QRS complexes can also be seen.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Pneumoperitoneum occurs when an intrathoracic air leak decompresses into the abdomen. It is typically asymptomatic and usually diagnosed on radiographic evaluation. It should, however, be differentiated from free abdominal air secondary to a ruptured viscus in which patients are usually symptomatic with signs and symptoms of peritonitis.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: In unstable neonates with progressive deterioration of their clinical status, transillumination of the chest might provide a quick bedside diagnostic tool and allow for immediate intervention before x-ray confirmation. The technique involves the use of a fiberoptic light probe that is placed on the infant’s chest wall while the room is darkened. In the presence of a large pneumothorax, the entire hemithorax on the affected side lights up, and the opposite side shows diminished transillumination because of lung compression on that side. In such cases, decompression should be accomplished without awaiting radiographic confirmation. However, in stable neonates, radiographic confirmation should always be sought before intervention. Inconclusive results or inexperience with the use of transillumination should also
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: be confirmed by x-ray before intervention. This allows for proper localization of the pneumothorax, as well as excluding other disorders that do not require evacuation, such as pneumomediastinum, CLE, or diaphragmatic hernia. Lung ultrasound is becoming more widely used as another bedside tool to make the diagnosis of pneumothorax faster than chest radiograph.143
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis is clear on radiographic evaluation of patients with a large or tension pneumothorax. Air accumulates between the parietal and visceral pleura, separating the lung from the chest wall and collapsing the ipsilateral lung. This can be seen as a curvilinear line silhouetting the collapsed lung (Fig. 67.7). External artifacts can also appear as a curvilinear line on chest radiograph; however, an artifact can be differentiated from a pneumothorax by its tendency to extend beyond the chest cavity in either direction. With a tension pneumothorax, the mediastinal structures, including the heart, are shifted away from the affected side. Lung collapse might not be complete, despite a severe pneumothorax in patients with RDS secondary to poor compliance of the affected lung. Smaller pneumothoraces might appear as a small sliver of free air lateral to the lung or above the diaphragm, causing the edge of the diaphragm or costophrenic angle to appear crisp. An anterior pneumothorax causes the affected lung to look translucent compared with the contralateral side. Confirmation of a small pneumothorax can be obtained with a lateral decubitus chest radiograph, where the unaffected side is dependent. As the free air rises, the reflection of the parietal pleura is seen clearly as a curvilinear line beyond which no lung markings are seen. This might also identify any contralateral pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Pneumomediastinum can be diagnosed on chest radiograph by elevation of the edge of the thymus from the pericardium by mediastinal free air in a characteristic crescent or
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: spinnaker sail configuration. A large pneumomediastinum can be differentiated from a pneumothorax by lateral decubitus radiographs as described earlier.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Pneumopericardium appears on plain chest radiograph as free air completely surrounding the heart but not extending beyond the aorta or pulmonary artery into the upper mediastinum. Although difficult to differentiate from a large pneumomediastinum, the presence of air between the heart and diaphragm is diagnostic of pneumopericardium (Fig. 67.8).
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: PIE is seen on chest radiograph as coarse, nonbranching radiolucencies that project toward the periphery of the lung in a disorganized fashion. This appearance must not be confused with an air bronchogram, a classic radiographic sign of RDS. Air bronchograms show long, smooth, branching radiolucencies that follow normal anatomic distributions similar to the bronchial tree. Pathologically, PIE is seen in lung tissue as multiple irregular, air-filled cysts varying in diameter from 1 mm to 1 cm, localized to interlobular septa, and extending radially from the hilum. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema can be localized to one lung or a lobe of a lung or can be diffuse bilateral disease. There is usually hyperinflation on the affected side that persists even after weaning ventilatory support.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Treatment of a pneumothorax depends on the severity of clinical presentation and whether it occurs during mechanical ventilation. In asymptomatic patients without underlying pulmonary disease, no treatment is required; however, close observation for worsening pneumothorax and development of respiratory symptoms is warranted. The pneumothorax usually resolves spontaneously in 1 to 2 days. Follow-up radiographs can be obtained as mandated by the clinical picture. The association of symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax with congenital renal malformations and the need for renal ultrasound evaluation in these patients are controversial. A review of 80 patients with spontaneous pneumothorax compared with normal controls showed no difference between the two groups in the rate of congenital renal malformations.144
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Only supportive care is needed in the treatment of symptomatic patients with a mild pneumothorax without evidence of respiratory failure. Theoretically, 100% oxygen given by a hood might lead to nitrogen washout and resolution or decrease in the size of the pneumothorax. Retrospective reviews showed no difference in time to resolution of pneumothorax in infants treated with 21% oxygen versus 100% oxygen versus somewhere in between.145,146 Oxygen is generally given only as needed to provide adequate oxygen saturations. Thoracocentesis is used for emergency evacuation of a large pneumothorax in unstable infants and might be the only treatment needed in nonventilated babies. However, recurrence of the pneumothorax should prompt the insertion of a chest tube. Thoracocentesis can also be used as a temporizing measure before chest tube insertion in ventilated infants.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: In ventilated patients with a large or tension pneumothorax, the initial management is to wean PIP and PEEP to reduce further air leak while preparing for chest tube placement. Deciding on which brand of chest tube and which insertion technique to use depends most importantly on experience and comfort level. The tube should be inserted under complete aseptic technique and positioned anterior to the affected lung. The position of the tube should be confirmed by anteroposterior and lateral chest radiographs. When placed correctly, there is immediate improvement in oxygenation in affected patients, and the tube should be connected to an underwater seal with continuous suctioning at 10 to 20 cmH2O. The chest tube should be secured when correct positioning is confirmed, with special attention given to preventing tension on the tube that could cause it to dislodge, particularly during radiologic examination. Chest tube insertion can be complicated by lung damage, which is usually diagnosed at autopsy, diaphragmatic paralysis secondary to phrenic nerve damage, or bleeding (Fig. 67.9). The use of a trocar or other sharp instrument during insertion should be avoided to decrease the chance of these complications. Once air bubbling stops, the chest tube should be clamped or water sealed overnight, and if the pneumothorax does not reaccumulate, the tube can be successfully removed. Isolated pneumomediastinum is usually
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: self-limiting and does not require intervention. However, these patients should be closely observed because a pneumothorax could develop.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Management of PIE can present a challenge. Increased support may lead to enlargement of the more compliant PIE cysts, which in turn compresses the relatively normal adjacent alveoli, causing worsening hypoxia and hypercapnia. The treatment strategy instead should target decreasing MAP while accepting higher CO2 levels and oxygen requirements to allow for collapse of the dilated interstitial cystic lesions and expansion of the normal alveoli. HFOV is an acceptable ventilatory strategy for PIE because of the lack of inflating volumes that tend to worsen the PIE. In the case of failure of conservative management and persistent PIE, different treatment strategies have been tried, especially in unilateral cases, with varying degrees of success, including single-lung ventilation.147
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: The occurrence of air leak is associated with increased incidence of mortality and morbidity. Together with the increased incidence of IVH mentioned earlier, VLBW infants who develop pneumothorax in the first 24 hours of life have been found to be 13 times more likely to die or develop bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Furthermore, ELBW infants with a pneumothorax who had a normal head ultrasound were more likely to develop cerebral palsy after controlling for other factors (odds ratio = 2.3).148 Therefore management strategies directed at avoiding the development of a pneumothorax should always be sought, including the use of minimal effective inspiratory pressures, low inspiratory time, high-frequency positive pressure ventilation, volume-targeted ventilation, early administration of surfactant in eligible patients, and rapid weaning of mechanical ventilation.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Assisted ventilation and oxygen therapy remain the standard of care for neonatal respiratory failure. In cases where infants develop intractable cardiorespiratory failure despite
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Respiratory Failure

paragraphs.text: maximal ventilatory and cardiovascular support, ECMO can be used to help improve chances of survival. In ECMO, techniques of cardiopulmonary bypass, modified from those originally developed for open-heart surgery, are used to provide prolonged respiratory and/or cardiovascular support. In newborns with hypoxic respiratory failure, this allows the lungs to rest and recover and prevents the often damaging effects of aggressive mechanical ventilation and 100% oxygen. Several randomized trials have demonstrated improved survival in infants supported with ECMO when compared to conventional therapy. The most rigorous prospective, randomized trial was conducted in the United Kingdom, where 185 infants with severe respiratory failure were randomized to ECMO or conventional ventilatory management.149 Survival in the ECMO-treated patients was 68% compared to 41% survival in the control arm (P = .0005), equivalent to one extra survivor for every three or four infants allocated to ECMO. Neurologic outcome was similar among survivors of either treatment arm, making it unlikely that ECMO contributed any added morbidity to this cohort of critically ill newborns.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Respiratory Failure

paragraphs.text: ECMO therapy became widely available to neonatal units in the late 1980s, and over the past three decades there have been changes in the patients who go on ECMO and the overall survival of those infants. The international Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) Registry reports a 5-year distribution of primary diagnoses and survival for patients undergoing ECMO support (Fig. 67.10). Over time, the ECMO caseload has changed. In the early years of ECMO, MAS was the most common reason for requiring ECMO, but more recently it is CDH. Survival has decreased from 80% to 85% in the 1980s to now 65% to 70% from the 2010s to 2020s. The length of time spent on ECMO more recently has also changed and is almost
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Respiratory Failure

paragraphs.text: double what it used to be (118 vs. 231 hours.).150 These changes are perhaps reflecting that infants who require ECMO support are sicker and more complex than those in the early days of ECMO, and possibly that we are now offering ECMO to patients who initially were not offered ECMO support.151
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Respiratory Failure

paragraphs.text: There are two modes of ECMO support, venoarterial (VA) and venovenous (VV). VA ECMO is able to provide both pulmonary and cardiac support, whereas VV ECMO provides only respiratory support, and patients must be able to maintain their native cardiac output. The decision for which mode to choose is dependent on the patient’s size, diagnosis, and clinical condition, as well as the center’s preference and experience.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: In VA ECMO, venous blood is drained from the right atrium by cannulating the right internal jugular vein with a catheter (8- to 14-French diameter) with its tip terminating in the mid-right atrium. Well-oxygenated blood is returned to the infant via a catheter (8- to 12-French) positioned in the ascending aortic arch through a right common carotid artery cannulation. Neonatal VV ECMO uses a dual lumen catheter that is inserted in the right internal jugular vein and terminates in the right atrium. The size of the dual lumen catheter for neonates is 13- or 15-French; thus one disadvantage of VV ECMO is that the infant usually has to weigh at least 2.5 kg in order to have an internal jugular large enough to fit the dual lumen catheter. Venous blood is drained from the right atrium and the well-oxygenated blood returning from the ECMO circuit is returned to the right atrium. The dual lumen catheter is positioned such that the arterial return port is directed toward the tricuspid
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: valve to encourage the flow of well-oxygenated blood into the right ventricle instead of being returned back to the ECMO circuit and preventing significant recirculation of that blood.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: Two types of pumps are available—roller and centrifugal—and which one is used is center dependent. Roller pumps are able to control the flow precisely in infants, but they are bulky and at risk for rupture. Centrifugal pumps are more compact and have less risk of rupture, but they have been associated with significant hemolysis in some neonatal patients. Hemolysis with centrifugal pumps has been associated with neurologic injury, acute kidney injury, and higher mortality.152,153 There has not been a rigorous trial comparing the two modes in neonates to recommend one over the other at this time.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: As the blood circulates through the artificial lung, gas exchange occurs against a filtered mixture of oxygen, CO2, and nitrogen in ambient air. The artificial lung is a hydrophobic, polymethylpentene hollow-fiber membrane that serves as a blood-gas interface, similar to the alveolar capillary membrane. Gas flows through the hollow fibers and venous blood flows around the outside of these fibers. Oxygen and carbon dioxide flow down their diffusion gradients, and gas exchange occurs across the hollow-fiber membrane. Similar to the native lung, blood leaving the membrane lung has a normal to low CO2 and a high PaO2, with oxygen saturation of 100%. The artificial lung also incorporates a heat exchanger to rewarm the oxygenated blood returning to the patient.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: Oxygenation is regulated by varying blood flow through the ECMO circuit. The higher the volume of cardiac output diverted through the membrane lung, the better the oxygen delivery from the ECMO circuit. Monitoring of the mixed venous oxygen saturation (SV̇O2) at the level of the right atrium is the best way to monitor for appropriate oxygenation on VA ECMO with a goal of 65% to 80%. On VV ECMO, due to recirculation the SV̇O2 is not an accurate measure of patient oxygenation; thus monitoring the patient’s saturations and PaO2 on blood gases is used. Blood flow through the ECMO circuit at a rate of 80 to 100 mL/kg/min on VA ECMO (higher on VV ECMO) is usually adequate to provide excellent cardiac and respiratory support with maintenance of adequate blood pressure and oxygenation.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: Systemic anticoagulation is required for ECMO and is achieved with unfractionated heparin or a direct thrombin inhibitor. In neonates, heparin remains more widely used. There is no consensus or ELSO recommendation regarding the best anticoagulation practice for neonatal respiratory ECMO. Usually a combination of multiple parameters such as activated clotting time (ACT), antifactor Xa assay, and partial thromboplastin times (PTTs), among others, are used.151
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: When the infant is placed on ECMO, ventilation and airway oxygen support are reduced to avoid further ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) while maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC) and allowing for pulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: hygiene. Wide practice variation exists with regard to ventilator settings used for “lung rest” during bypass support, and more research is needed to provide evidence-based best-practice guidance for rest settings during ECMO. A retrospective cohort study using the ELSO database found that the use of conventional ventilation compared to highfrequency ventilation and the use of a mid-PEEP (7–9 cmH2O) or high-PEEP (10–12 cmH2O) strategy compared to a low-PEEP strategy (4–6 cmH2O) were associated with a shorter time on ECMO.154 Currently, ELSO recommends using a PIP of 15 to 10 cmH2O, PEEP of 5 to 10 cmH2O and lower with air leak, a rate of 12 to 20 breaths per minute, inspiratory time of 0.5 to 1 seconds, and fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 0.21 to 0.3.151 As lung function improves and pulmonary hypertension abates, the mixed venous saturation and PaO2 improve, and weaning from ECMO support can commence. When the infant has reached minimal ECMO support and is able to be adequately supported with acceptable ventilator settings, the patient can be decannulated. Upon removal of the cannulas, the vessels are often ligated; however, in shorter ECMO runs (typically <7 days), a surgeon may consider vessel reconstruction. Although studies have demonstrated that reconstructing the right common carotid does not pose an increased risk of embolic events and neurodevelopmental impairment, there is no consensus on the utility of carotid reconstruction.155-157
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: Although VV ECMO is the predominant mode of ECMO for respiratory support reported in the ELSO database, VA ECMO support continues to be the most frequently used mode for neonatal respiratory ECMO. In 2020, only 11% of neonatal respiratory ECMO cases were VV.150 The reason for this is likely multifactorial and includes size constraints, recent lack of VV cannulas, and EMCO team comfort with VV ECMO. Advantages of VV bypass include avoidance of carotid artery cannulation, which is highly desirable, and maintenance of normal pulmonary blood flow. The major disadvantage is that, unlike VA bypass, VV ECMO does not provide cardiac support. The severity of cardiac dysfunction in ECMO-sick patients is highly variable, and often the heart function will improve when adequate oxygen content is restored on VV ECMO. Survival on VV ECMO is no worse than VA, and in some reports may even be better than VA ECMO. However, these retrospective studies are limited by selection bias, as VA patients tend to be smaller and sicker when going on ECMO.158 Only 10% to 12% of VV cases require conversion from VV to VA support should the patient’s cardiac output prove to be subpar.150 Therefore VV bypass should always be the first consideration in infants whose primary diagnosis is pulmonary disease.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: The cumulative experience of many ECMO centers has resulted in the establishment of guidelines that are currently used to decide whether ECMO support is appropriate.151
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: These are described in Box 67.5, and other clarifications follow.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Preterm newborns with respiratory failure carry a higher risk for intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) compared with term infants at baseline, and this risk is heightened with systemic anticoagulation required during ECMO support. Furthermore, changes in cerebral blood flow patterns associated with cardiopulmonary bypass can also place the immature brain at increased risk for bleeding.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: In the early ECMO trials, premature infants less than 35 weeks’ gestation had an 89% incidence of spontaneous ICH associated with heparinization.159 Subsequent studies (all retrospective) revisiting this issue reported improvement in outcome but confirmed increased rates of ICH in preterm infants. When compared to term infants, late preterm infants had higher mortality and increased morbidities, including ICH.160 A study comparing ECMO outcome at 34 weeks’ gestation to that of preterms between 29 and 33 weeks’ gestation, reported survival was greater at 34 weeks’ gestation (58%) compared to 48% survival in the <34-week cohort. The rate of ICH peaked at 44% at 31 weeks and decreased incrementally to 17% by 34 weeks.161 Although it is generally accepted that ECMO should be used for those infants of 34 weeks’ gestation or greater, an earlier gestational age could be considered for ECMO after discussion with the team and the family with the understanding of associated risks.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Severe IVH and uncontrollable bleeding are also contraindications for ECMO. Severe IVH (grades III and IV) are likely to expand when the infant is anticoagulated for ECMO and worsen long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Infants in severe respiratory failure must have an echocardiogram to rule out congenital heart disease as the underlying cause for refractory hypoxemia. In some instances, the degree of hypoxemia is not easily explained based on the heart lesion alone (e.g., in a newborn with an atrioventricular canal complicated by meconium aspiration or sepsis). In such an instance, ECMO can provide cardiovascular support to stabilize the patient until the reversible component of the lung disease is no longer an issue. Similarly, an infant with suspected cyanotic congenital heart disease
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: may present with profound cyanosis and cardiogenic shock despite the use of prostaglandins and inotropes. Preoperative ECMO can stabilize such infants who are believed to have reparable cardiac defects but who are deemed to be poor surgical candidates by virtue of their clinical instability.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: ECMO is an invasive procedure used for infants with hypoxic respiratory failure unresponsive to optimal conventional therapy. In the early days of ECMO (1975–1995), infants with an 80% mortality risk based on retrospective data at the time were considered candidates for ECMO. Over the past 30 years, however, much has changed in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) management of infants with hypoxic respiratory failure, including ventilator management and adjuvant therapies for pulmonary hypertension, as well as the choices of optimal blood gas parameters. Hyperventilation, alkali therapy, and muscle paralysis are no longer recommended, as serious side effects are associated with each of these interventions. It is therefore difficult to know what might constitute an 80% mortality risk in the ECMO-sick newborn today. Box 67.6 offers guidelines utilized by ECMO intensivists for deciding when bypass is likely needed. One of the most difficult decisions faced by neonatologists who are not in an ECMO center is when to refer a newborn in respiratory failure to an ECMO center. Because of the volatile nature of PPHN, the risk of sudden cardiorespiratory decompensation and death remains high in any infant not responding favorably to conventional supportive measures. Likewise, transporting these unstable babies is problematic, with one series reporting 25% mortality among ECMO transports before inhaled NO was available.162,163
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: It is essential that ECMO referrals be made as expeditiously as possible and preferably before the baby reaches ECMO-eligible criteria. Early and frequent telephone contact with an ECMO physician to discuss the details of each case can help establish transport criteria agreeable to both parties. Expert opinion has stated that, when the oxygenation index is greater than 25, a non-ECMO center should
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: at least be in discussion with an ECMO center to determine the optimal time to transport the infant.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: CDH is the most common indication for neonates with hypoxic respiratory failure to receive ECMO support. ECMO gives these infants time for their pulmonary hypertension and/or cardiac dysfunction to improve, but only about half of the infants with CDH placed on ECMO survive.150,164 There has been wide variability across centers as to when to use ECMO in the CDH population, which infants are candidates, when the CDH should be repaired, and the mode of ECMO that should be used. Recently, ELSO provided a guideline for the use of ECMO in the CDH population which is summarized below.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: ECMO is reserved for patients with CDH who are failing optimal medical treatment, including a strategy of pressure-limited (gentle) ventilation to minimize ventilatorassociated lung injury and optimizing the medical management of their pulmonary hypertension. The initiation criteria should be the same as for neonates without CDH. Consensus indications based on recent expert opinion are summarized in Box 67.7. Contraindications are similar to those for patients without CDH. In addition, infants with
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: CDH+ (co-existing additional major anomalies, chromosomal aberrations, or syndromes) have a significantly lower survival than infants with isolated CDH, and it may be reasonable not to offer ECMO to those patients.67 The survival among CDH infants treated with ECMO over the last 5 years is 56%, which has not changed much over time and reflects the highest mortality among neonatal etiologies of respiratory failure reported in the ELSO Registry.150 In 1991, survival in this cohort was 64%. The reason for this decline is not entirely clear, but it is thought that potentially those infants requiring ECMO are sicker with higher mortality and lengths of ECMO runs.165
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: Which mode of ECMO to use for CDH patients and when to repair the CDH remain topics of controversy. Proponents of VV ECMO comment on the improved delivery of oxygen to the lungs and decreased neurologic complications. Studies have demonstrated that CDH patients can be successfully managed on VV ECMO; however, no survival benefit has been shown.164
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: The optimum timing for repair of the hernia in ECMOsick patients remains unclear, however, because of variability among centers and lack of convincing data on how best to proceed. The current guidelines recommend it for infants who can be decannulated or weaned off ECMO, but there may be benefit to delaying repair until after the infant is off ECMO. For patients with a severe CDH phenotype, very early repair while on ECMO may afford a survival advantage because non-repairs will be avoided, complication rates may be lower than with late repair, and early correction of the mechanical contributors to pulmonary and vascular pathophysiology may facilitate weaning off support.30 What is important is that the decision takes into consideration the challenges associated with operating on ECMO and potential issues from delaying repair until the infant is near to being and hopefully able to be decannulated.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: The true impact of ECMO on survival and long-term outcome in newborns with CDH is difficult to ascertain. Infants with CDH who receive ECMO support appear to have a higher risk and greater severity of neurologic morbidity compared to those who have not received ECMO or those who received ECMO for other causes of hypoxemic respiratory failure.166–168 Among neonatal ECMO patients who survived to hospital discharge, patients with CDH had a 74% 5-year survival compared to 98% survival in patients with MAS.169 Most deaths in the CDH cohort were caused by chronic lung disease.170 It is difficult to differentiate whether these outcomes are associated with the underlying disease process or their need for ECMO support. All survivors should have multidisciplinary follow-up that includes neurodevelopmental assessments.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: More than 33,000 infants have been treated for respiratory failure in more than 400 ECMO centers worldwide for an overall survival to discharge of 73%.150 The outcome
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: of these children compares favorably with that of term and near-term infants surviving severe respiratory compromise and PPHN with conventional management.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: A valid criticism of early ECMO follow-up studies was the lack of proper control data—that is, the outcome of infants with severe respiratory compromise who were managed during the ECMO era with conventional treatment alone. Such control data are essential for distinguishing morbid outcome caused by the underlying disease process and NICU management of respiratory failure, or both, from the morbidity that is secondary to the ECMO procedure itself.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: Single-center, early outcome studies found that patients treated with ECMO had higher survival, less chronic lung disease, and less reactive airway disease when compared to the neonates managed with conventional medical therapy. There were no differences between neurodevelopmental outcomes at 8 and 20 months of age.171 In another study at 12 to 30 months of age, the mean developmental scores of ECMO survivors were similar to those for infants who survived without ECMO. Neuroimaging abnormalities or diagnosis of bronchopulmonary dysplasia each independently predicted adverse neurodevelopmental outcome regardless of treatment strategies used in the NICU.172 The UK Collaborative ECMO Trial Group found that there was no difference in cognitive function, with 76% of the children having a cognitive level within normal range, and there were similar rates of learning difficulties between the groups, notably difficulties with spatial and processing tasks at 7 years of age. Similar to the other early studies, children who were treated conventionally continued to have higher respiratory morbidities, including wheezing and inhaler use. Conventionally treated children also had more behavioral problems, typically hyperactivity. These results are equivalent to one additional child surviving without severe disability for every four to five children referred for ECMO.173
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: The majority of more recent long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of ECMO survivors has been reported from a nationwide prospective follow-up program in The Netherlands. The severity of critical illness and the underlying disease that resulted in cardiorespiratory failure and the need for ECMO are the primary determinants of adverse long-term outcomes.174 About 25% of neonatal ECMO survivors will have neuropsychologic deficits that may have potential impact on academic performance in later life. After serial longitudinal cognitive testing at 2, 5, and 8 years, the Dutch group found that intelligence was stable over time; however, more of the survivors required special education supports compared to a normal Dutch reference cohort. Increased behavior and attention issues were also cited. There were also problems with visual and spatial information processing and attention/concentration issues.167 The group also reported that a small cohort of the adolescent ECMO survivors were at risk of verbal, visualspatial, and working memory problems.175 Motor delays also become apparent with time. At 5, 8, and 12 years of age, motor function was normal in 74%, 75%, and 41%,
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: respectively. The significant decline in motor scores at 12 years was most pronounced in children with chronic lung disease and CDH. Exercise capacity (based on the Bruce treadmill protocol) also worsened significantly over time.176 The significance in such decline in motor performance and exercise capacity is troublesome and points to a serious need for long-term follow-up of these children not only throughout their pediatric years but also into adulthood. In the United States, unfortunately, we do not have neurodevelopmental follow-up to compare to the UK and Netherlands programs. In 2016, a survey assessment of a cohort of 142 adult (>18 years, born before 1994) survivors of neonatal ECMO in the United States was published. Although this self-reported outcome was largely favorable, this study represented only a small fraction (<2%) of neonatal ECMO survivors who have reached adulthood.177 Finding these patients, particularly those not receiving routine medical care, will prove formidable.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: Thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities are a rare group of conditions that can cause respiratory distress by restriction of thoracic volume. They include a number of entities incompatible with life or life limiting. In this group of diseases are those with hypoplasia of the ribs and thorax, including asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Jeune syndrome), thanatophoric dysplasia, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta type II, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (chondroectodermal dysplasia), hypophosphatasia, spondylothoracic dysostosis, and cerebrocostomandibular syndrome.178
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Respiratory distress caused by structural abnormalities of the chest wall should be readily apparent. However, marked narrowing of the thorax can result in what appears to be a distended abdomen, and the respiratory problem can be erroneously attributed to an intra-abdominal pathologic condition. The presence of other associated anomalies (for example, short-limbed dwarfism), together with close observation of respiratory excursions, examination of the bony thorax, and measurement of the circumference of the chest, establishes the diagnosis even before a review is made of the thoracic and skeletal radiographs.
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: With structural abnormalities of the chest wall, asphyxia and respiratory distress are present from birth. The infants are cyanotic and tachypneic and demonstrate severe retractions and, characteristically, a virtually immobile chest. Diaphragmatic excursions are prominent; thus respiration appears entirely abdominal. Pulmonary hypoplasia accompanies the thoracic dystrophy, and radiographically the lungs can appear airless.
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Infants with asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, thanatophoric dwarfism, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, or Ellis-van Creveld syndrome have thoracic radiographs with a squared-off appearance, and the posterior rib arcs all appear to be the same length. The clavicles
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: appear very high, and the diaphragms are low (Fig. 67.11). The transverse diameter of the thorax can appear diminished in comparison with the vertical diameter. On a lateral view, the ribs are very short and can appear clubbed anteriorly. The anteroposterior diameter of the thorax is decreased. The lungs may be poorly aerated, infiltrates are often present, and the heart might appear enlarged. Differentiating among the various syndromes of thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities usually is accomplished by means of a skeletal survey. Multiple fractures and bone demineralization are characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta and hypophosphatasia. Definitive diagnosis is made with the help of radiologists and geneticists, and there is growing knowledge of the genetic mutations involved in the various skeletal dysplasias.178
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Jeune syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia with multiorgan involvement. The genetic etiologies are very heterogeneous and result from autosomal mutations in one of at least 17 genes, including DYNC2H1, DYNC2LI1, TTC21B, IFT140, and IFT80 genes, among others. These genes encode proteins involved in the formation or function of cilia, which play a role in the signaling pathways important for the growth, proliferation, and differentiation of cells during the formation and maintenance of cartilage and bone.178 The hallmarks of asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy are extreme constriction and narrowing of the thorax and pulmonary hypoplasia, short ribs, and variable shortening of the limbs with abnormalities of the bones of the pelvis and extremities. The thorax is relatively immobile, and the ribs are horizontally directed and short with bulbous ends. In addition to the thoracic abnormalities, the infants have trident iliac bones with a double-notch appearance of the acetabulum. Associated anomalies include polydactyly and deformed teeth. Renal abnormalities may be present, and renal failure can occur later in life.
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: These infants usually present with respiratory distress and recurrent respiratory infections during the neonatal period. It has been reported that 60% to 80% of cases are
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: fatal in early childhood, but if they survive the early years, the patients’ respiratory problems tend to decrease with age, and a subset of children affected by this disorder can have long-term survival.179
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: Thanatophoric dysplasia (see Chapter 29) is the most common form of lethal skeletal dysplasia. It is caused by de novo mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and is an autosomal dominant condition.180 Appearance at birth is characteristic and includes striking micromelia in association with a normal trunk, a large head with frontal bossing, and a narrow thorax. The radiographic findings include severely flattened vertebral bodies with markedly widened intervertebral disk spaces, small iliac rings, and flaring of the metaphyses of the long bones. There is a high incidence of polyhydramnios, and the infants often present in the breech position.
paragraphs.heading: Thanatophoric Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Infants present at birth with severe pulmonary insufficiency, requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive neonatal care. Immediate and accurate diagnosis is important in guiding medical decisions about continuation of support. The majority of infants die in the neonatal period, but a recent report from Japan has described survival beyond the neonatal period with ventilator management.181
paragraphs.heading: Thanatophoric Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Phrenic nerve injury with paralysis of the diaphragm is an unusual cause of neonatal respiratory distress. It is usually associated with birth trauma and presents in association with an ipsilateral brachial plexus injury. When occurring on the right, Horner syndrome can coexist; however, injury can also occur after cardiovascular or thoracic surgeries or following invasive procedures. The injuries are observed in infants who are large for gestational age, especially following shoulder dystocia or difficult breech extractions. Fractures of the humerus or clavicle are often observed. The nerve roots of C3 to C5 are stretched, with lateral hyperextension and traction on the neck. Recovery depends on the degree of injury; avulsion results in permanent injury, and diaphragmatic eventration secondary to muscle atrophy ensues. Lesser injury or edema of the nerve roots results in a spectrum of respiratory symptoms that can include cyanosis, weak cry, tachypnea, or apnea. On radiographic examination, the involved hemidiaphragm is elevated, and atelectasis is usually observed on that side. The heart and mediastinum are shifted away from the affected side (Fig. 67.12). Ultrasonographic or fluoroscopic evaluation should be diagnostic and reveal paradoxic movement of the diaphragm with elevation during inspiration and descent with expiration. Congenital eventration of the diaphragm also results in an elevated hemidiaphragm with paradoxical movement. Secondary pneumonia is the major source of morbidity and mortality. Treatment of phrenic nerve palsy initially is supportive
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: and, in the absence of avulsion, spontaneous resolution is to be expected. Surgical plication of the diaphragm might be required for selected infants with avulsion.182,183
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: • Not all respiratory distress after birth is due to respiratory
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: distress syndrome. • The degree of respiratory distress due to these other causes

67 Spectrum of Neonatal Respiratory Disorders

### MOIRA A. CROWLEY

Multiple pathophysiologic mechanisms can present with pulmonary manifestations in term and preterm infants. The clinical picture is most commonly dominated by respiratory distress, which presents as tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions, cyanosis, and hypoxemia. However, apnea and hypoventilation are also common. In preterm infants, these manifestations are commonly associated with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), as discussed in Chapter 65. Nonpulmonary etiologies of respiratory distress include thermal instability, circulatory problems, cardiac disease, neuromuscular disorders, sepsis, anemia or polycythemia, and methemoglobinemia (Box 67.1). This chapter presents an overview of the many other respiratory disorders that can affect preterm and term infants. It also discusses treatment strategies for these respiratory disorders including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for severe cardiorespiratory failure resulting from some of these diagnoses.

### Developmental Diseases

### Pulmonary Underdevelopment: Pulmonary Agenesis, Aplasia, and Hypoplasia

Abnormal lung development varies from mild hypoplasia to agenesis of a single lobe or whole lung. Agenesis of the lung is a rare congenital anomaly defined as the total absence of pulmonary parenchyma, its supporting vasculature, and bronchi after the bifurcation.1 Complete agenesis of the lung is usually unilateral (90%), although dysgenesis of the other lung has been reported.2 Pulmonary aplasia is a subset of pulmonary agenesis, defined by the presence of a blindending, rudimentary bronchus without associated lung parenchyma or pulmonary vasculature.3 It has been hypothesized that pulmonary agenesis is vascular in origin, most likely resulting from a disruption of the dorsal aortic arch blood flow during the fourth week of gestation. Although lung agenesis can be an isolated finding, in as many as 50% to 76% cases it is associated with other congenital malformations, including urogenital, vertebral, cardiac, and

gastrointestinal, as well as malformations of the first and second branchial arch derivatives and radial ray defects.4 As a result, pulmonary agenesis has been considered a subset of the VACTERL (vertebral, anal atresia, cardiac defect, tracheo-esophageal fistula, renal anomalies, limb anomalies) sequence and, when involving the ipsilateral branchial arch or radial ray malformations, Goldenhar syndrome.2

Diagnosis is confirmed on antenatal ultrasound by the presence of mediastinal shift in the absence of a diaphragmatic hernia or lung mass. Antenatal echocardiogram reveals total absence of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches on the affected side. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination can confirm the diagnosis, evaluate the size of the remaining lung, and evaluate the presence of other congenital malformations. After delivery, diagnosis of infants with unilateral pulmonary agenesis can be suspected by decreased breath sounds and displacement of the mediastinum to the affected side. Some breath sounds, however, may be audible over the affected side if a portion of normal lung, which usually has undergone compensatory hypertrophy, has herniated across the midline into the affected hemithorax. The radiographic appearance of a radiopaque hemithorax helps confirm the diagnosis, and accompanying vertebral defects are not uncommon (Fig. 67.1). Treatment is largely supportive, and the prognosis depends on the presence or absence of other anomalies; those with isolated pulmonary agenesis have better survival.4

Pulmonary hypoplasia is the result of deficient or incomplete development of the lung parenchyma leading to decreased number of distal airways, alveoli, and associated pulmonary vessels. It can be classified as either primary, caused by intrinsic failure of normal lung development, or secondary, caused by a multitude of different pathologic processes that interfere with normal lung development. Diagnosis of pulmonary hypoplasia is made pathologically by measuring the lung-to-body ratio; however, this truly only captures those with lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. Methods to diagnose pulmonary hypoplasia antenatally in those fetuses at risk for developing pulmonary hypoplasia because of associated findings have been reported and include the use of prenatal ultrasound techniques and fetal MRI. Ultrasound measurement techniques include thoracic circumference (TC) corrected for gestational age or femur length, TC:abdominal circumference ratio, and thoracic:heart area. These techniques, however, measure the thoracic wall rather than lung parenchyma itself and have inadequate positive and negative predictive values to be a reliable tool for predicting pulmonary hypoplasia in isolation. More recently, measurement of lung volume using three-dimensional ultrasound has been reported, but, even in the most experienced hands, 8% to 48% of cases did not have a calculable lung volume on at least one side.5 MRI has shown promise in predicting pulmonary hypoplasia, especially in the setting of CDH, but seems to be no better for other causes of pulmonary hypoplasia.5 Pathologic examination of the hypoplastic lung can show a low ratio of lung to body weight, low DNA content, or decreased radial alveolar count. Peripheral bronchioles are decreased in number, as are the pulmonary arterioles, which often exhibit hypertrophy of medial smooth muscle, a predisposition to persistent pulmonary hypertension.
