A valid criticism of early ECMO follow-up studies was the lack of proper control data—that is, the outcome of infants with severe respiratory compromise who were managed during the ECMO era with conventional treatment alone. Such control data are essential for distinguishing morbid outcome caused by the underlying disease process and NICU management of respiratory failure, or both, from the morbidity that is secondary to the ECMO procedure itself.

Single-center, early outcome studies found that patients treated with ECMO had higher survival, less chronic lung disease, and less reactive airway disease when compared to the neonates managed with conventional medical therapy. There were no differences between neurodevelopmental outcomes at 8 and 20 months of age.171 In another study at 12 to 30 months of age, the mean developmental scores of ECMO survivors were similar to those for infants who survived without ECMO. Neuroimaging abnormalities or diagnosis of bronchopulmonary dysplasia each independently predicted adverse neurodevelopmental outcome regardless of treatment strategies used in the NICU.172 The UK Collaborative ECMO Trial Group found that there was no difference in cognitive function, with 76% of the children having a cognitive level within normal range, and there were similar rates of learning difficulties between the groups, notably difficulties with spatial and processing tasks at 7 years of age. Similar to the other early studies, children who were treated conventionally continued to have higher respiratory morbidities, including wheezing and inhaler use. Conventionally treated children also had more behavioral problems, typically hyperactivity. These results are equivalent to one additional child surviving without severe disability for every four to five children referred for ECMO.173

The majority of more recent long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of ECMO survivors has been reported from a nationwide prospective follow-up program in The Netherlands. The severity of critical illness and the underlying disease that resulted in cardiorespiratory failure and the need for ECMO are the primary determinants of adverse long-term outcomes.174 About 25% of neonatal ECMO survivors will have neuropsychologic deficits that may have potential impact on academic performance in later life. After serial longitudinal cognitive testing at 2, 5, and 8 years, the Dutch group found that intelligence was stable over time; however, more of the survivors required special education supports compared to a normal Dutch reference cohort. Increased behavior and attention issues were also cited. There were also problems with visual and spatial information processing and attention/concentration issues.167 The group also reported that a small cohort of the adolescent ECMO survivors were at risk of verbal, visualspatial, and working memory problems.175 Motor delays also become apparent with time. At 5, 8, and 12 years of age, motor function was normal in 74%, 75%, and 41%,

respectively. The significant decline in motor scores at 12 years was most pronounced in children with chronic lung disease and CDH. Exercise capacity (based on the Bruce treadmill protocol) also worsened significantly over time.176 The significance in such decline in motor performance and exercise capacity is troublesome and points to a serious need for long-term follow-up of these children not only throughout their pediatric years but also into adulthood. In the United States, unfortunately, we do not have neurodevelopmental follow-up to compare to the UK and Netherlands programs. In 2016, a survey assessment of a cohort of 142 adult (>18 years, born before 1994) survivors of neonatal ECMO in the United States was published. Although this self-reported outcome was largely favorable, this study represented only a small fraction (<2%) of neonatal ECMO survivors who have reached adulthood.177 Finding these patients, particularly those not receiving routine medical care, will prove formidable.

### Rib Cage Abnormalities

Thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities are a rare group of conditions that can cause respiratory distress by restriction of thoracic volume. They include a number of entities incompatible with life or life limiting. In this group of diseases are those with hypoplasia of the ribs and thorax, including asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Jeune syndrome), thanatophoric dysplasia, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta type II, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (chondroectodermal dysplasia), hypophosphatasia, spondylothoracic dysostosis, and cerebrocostomandibular syndrome.178

Respiratory distress caused by structural abnormalities of the chest wall should be readily apparent. However, marked narrowing of the thorax can result in what appears to be a distended abdomen, and the respiratory problem can be erroneously attributed to an intra-abdominal pathologic condition. The presence of other associated anomalies (for example, short-limbed dwarfism), together with close observation of respiratory excursions, examination of the bony thorax, and measurement of the circumference of the chest, establishes the diagnosis even before a review is made of the thoracic and skeletal radiographs.

With structural abnormalities of the chest wall, asphyxia and respiratory distress are present from birth. The infants are cyanotic and tachypneic and demonstrate severe retractions and, characteristically, a virtually immobile chest. Diaphragmatic excursions are prominent; thus respiration appears entirely abdominal. Pulmonary hypoplasia accompanies the thoracic dystrophy, and radiographically the lungs can appear airless.

Infants with asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, thanatophoric dwarfism, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, or Ellis-van Creveld syndrome have thoracic radiographs with a squared-off appearance, and the posterior rib arcs all appear to be the same length. The clavicles

### Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

Jeune syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia with multiorgan involvement. The genetic etiologies are very heterogeneous and result from autosomal mutations in one of at least 17 genes, including DYNC2H1, DYNC2LI1, TTC21B, IFT140, and IFT80 genes, among others. These genes encode proteins involved in the formation or function of cilia, which play a role in the signaling pathways important for the growth, proliferation, and differentiation of cells during the formation and maintenance of cartilage and bone.178 The hallmarks of asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy are extreme constriction and narrowing of the thorax and pulmonary hypoplasia, short ribs, and variable shortening of the limbs with abnormalities of the bones of the pelvis and extremities. The thorax is relatively immobile, and the ribs are horizontally directed and short with bulbous ends. In addition to the thoracic abnormalities, the infants have trident iliac bones with a double-notch appearance of the acetabulum. Associated anomalies include polydactyly and deformed teeth. Renal abnormalities may be present, and renal failure can occur later in life.

These infants usually present with respiratory distress and recurrent respiratory infections during the neonatal period. It has been reported that 60% to 80% of cases are

fatal in early childhood, but if they survive the early years, the patients’ respiratory problems tend to decrease with age, and a subset of children affected by this disorder can have long-term survival.179

### Thanatophoric Dysplasia

Thanatophoric dysplasia (see Chapter 29) is the most common form of lethal skeletal dysplasia. It is caused by de novo mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and is an autosomal dominant condition.180 Appearance at birth is characteristic and includes striking micromelia in association with a normal trunk, a large head with frontal bossing, and a narrow thorax. The radiographic findings include severely flattened vertebral bodies with markedly widened intervertebral disk spaces, small iliac rings, and flaring of the metaphyses of the long bones. There is a high incidence of polyhydramnios, and the infants often present in the breech position.

Infants present at birth with severe pulmonary insufficiency, requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive neonatal care. Immediate and accurate diagnosis is important in guiding medical decisions about continuation of support. The majority of infants die in the neonatal period, but a recent report from Japan has described survival beyond the neonatal period with ventilator management.181

### Phrenic Nerve Injury

Phrenic nerve injury with paralysis of the diaphragm is an unusual cause of neonatal respiratory distress. It is usually associated with birth trauma and presents in association with an ipsilateral brachial plexus injury. When occurring on the right, Horner syndrome can coexist; however, injury can also occur after cardiovascular or thoracic surgeries or following invasive procedures. The injuries are observed in infants who are large for gestational age, especially following shoulder dystocia or difficult breech extractions. Fractures of the humerus or clavicle are often observed. The nerve roots of C3 to C5 are stretched, with lateral hyperextension and traction on the neck. Recovery depends on the degree of injury; avulsion results in permanent injury, and diaphragmatic eventration secondary to muscle atrophy ensues. Lesser injury or edema of the nerve roots results in a spectrum of respiratory symptoms that can include cyanosis, weak cry, tachypnea, or apnea. On radiographic examination, the involved hemidiaphragm is elevated, and atelectasis is usually observed on that side. The heart and mediastinum are shifted away from the affected side (Fig. 67.12). Ultrasonographic or fluoroscopic evaluation should be diagnostic and reveal paradoxic movement of the diaphragm with elevation during inspiration and descent with expiration. Congenital eventration of the diaphragm also results in an elevated hemidiaphragm with paradoxical movement. Secondary pneumonia is the major source of morbidity and mortality.
